For noncompact locally compact Hausdorff X, checked the topology directly: unions and finite intersections of compact-complement neighborhoods remain of that form, using finite unions and closed subsets of compact sets. For compactness, an open cover of X⁺ has a member containing ∞, whose complement is compact; finitely cover that complement and add the ∞-member. For Hausdorffness, separate two X-points in X, and separate x from ∞ by a neighborhood of x with compact closure, whose ∞-neighborhood is its compact-complement. X is open and dense because every nonempty ∞-neighborhood contains X\K and X is noncompact. Coordinator also checked uniqueness: in any compact Hausdorff extension by one point, complements of neighborhoods of that point are compact subsets of X; conversely any compact K in X is closed in the extension, so its complement is such a neighborhood. This determines the topology. Stereographic projection gives the Euclidean examples: y maps to (2y/(1+norm(y)^2),(norm(y)^2-1)/(1+norm(y)^2)); infinity maps to the north pole, and complements of compact sets give continuity there. The real line and complex plane are the n=1 and n=2 cases. If X is compact its complement at infinity is the singleton, which is isolated and prevents density.

entries.evidence: Coordinator checked the full statement in the metric subspace K. Compact implies sequentially compact: if no subsequence converges, each x has a ball containing only finitely many sequence indices (otherwise choose successive indices in radius 1/n balls); a finite subcover contradicts infinitely many indices. Conversely sequential compactness implies total boundedness: failure gives an epsilon-separated sequence, which has no convergent subsequence. Every open cover has a Lebesgue number: otherwise choose x_n with B_K(x_n,1/n) contained in no cover member; a convergent subsequence tends to x, and a member containing a ball B_K(x,r) eventually contains those small balls, contradiction. A finite epsilon-net for epsilon smaller than that Lebesgue number now supplies a finite subcover. No countability of the given open cover is assumed. The restriction to metric spaces is essential.

entries.evidence: The inspected paper's §2 proves injectivity of the affine-octonionic-line Radon transform by an explicit inversion formula and states the resulting density of line-supported distributions in Corollary 2.1.4. Its §1.3 and the transitivity argument in §3.2 support the affine-line and Spin(9) symmetry statements.

The factorization at a point with multiplicity m and the local argument-principle/winding argument establish that every image neighborhood contains a neighborhood of f(a), hence f(U) is open. Injectivity forces m=1, so the inverse derivative is holomorphic as stated.

The unique local factorization f=(z-a)^m u with u(a) nonzero gives the stated zero/pole signs; multiplication and quotient orders add/subtract, and integrating f'/f on a small positive circle returns m by direct Laurent expansion.

Restriction to every complex affine line gives the standard definition; for C^2 functions, vanishing mixed derivatives is equivalent to vanishing on every complex direction, and this makes both u and -u plurisubharmonic. The local real-part representation follows by integrating the holomorphic differential du components.

The linewise sub-mean definition and C^2 Levi-form criterion have the correct quantifiers and normalization. The trace identity Δu=4 tr(u_{z_j ar z_k}) gives ordinary subharmonicity, and log|F| is PSH by the standard distributional zero-divisor argument.

With S(w)=w'''/w'−(3/2)(w''/w')^2, the Schwarzian chain rule for a projective coordinate f gives R_z=R_w(w)(w')^2+S(w), exactly the displayed convention. Postcomposition by Möbius maps leaves the coefficient unchanged; the stated sign/factor warning correctly fixes convention dependence.

Subtracting the two projective-connection transformation laws cancels the Schwarzian and leaves the (w')^2 transition law for a quadratic differential. Adding any holomorphic quadratic differential preserves the law, proving free transitive translation when the set is nonempty.

The max/min identity has the necessary continuity and minimum-PSH hypothesis. Alesker's quaternionic valuation paper, Theorem 3.2.1, supplies the corresponding Błocki identity and mixed polarization; the support-function paragraph correctly adds the convex-union/intersection condition needed for max/min support functions.

The generalized contour statement has the correct meromorphic-domain condition Ind(γ,a)=0 outside D and finite nonzero-index pole sum. The simple positive contour specialization and the logarithmic-derivative/argument-principle application follow immediately from the winding-number form.

The theorem has the required nonempty proper plane-domain and simple-connectivity hypotheses. The normalization f(a)=0 and f'(a)>0 gives uniqueness, while the excluded whole-plane and boundary-regularity remarks correctly state the scope.

The two charts z and w=1/z give the standard compact Riemann surface and match the projective-line coordinates [z0:z1]. Stereographic projection is conformal, sphere automorphisms are Möbius maps, and meromorphic functions correspond to holomorphic sphere-valued maps with poles sent to infinity.

The strict boundary inequality prevents f+tg from vanishing on γ for 0≤t≤1, so its winding number is constant; the argument principle then gives equal interior zero counts with multiplicity. The contour and holomorphy hypotheses are sufficient for the stated form.

For y''+(q/2)y=0 and f=y1/y2, direct differentiation gives S(f)=q and the Wronskian shows f' never vanishes where y2 is finite; poles are handled as a meromorphic sphere map. Changing the solution basis acts by Möbius postcomposition, and the local square-root converse has the correct sign.

Substitution into S(h)=h'''/h'−(3/2)(h''/h')² yields S(f∘g)=(S(f)∘g)(g')²+S(g). Since direct calculation gives S(T)=0 for Möbius T, the postcomposition and projective-connection transformation statements follow.

The definition has the standard local-univalence hypothesis f'≠0 and formula S(f)=f'''/f'−(3/2)(f''/f')². The logarithmic-derivative rewrite is algebraically correct, and the scope warning appropriately distinguishes the meromorphic treatment at critical points.

Cross-ratio normalization sends any ordered triple of distinct sphere points to (1,0,∞), giving existence; a Möbius map fixing three points is the identity, giving uniqueness. Bearden's inspected Möbius chapter identifies the transformations with the orientation-preserving conformal sphere maps (the author-hosted notes reproduce the extension argument), while the ordered-quadruple orbit criterion follows from the cross-ratio invariant.

entries.evidence: Whole section reviewed: navigation covers the declared Lie-group/Lie-algebra, representation, structure, exceptional, and Lorentz topics; links are organized under coherent headings and no mathematical assertions beyond scope labels require correction.

The zero-bracket definition is equivalent to vanishing derived algebra, full center, and zero adjoint map. The connected-group remark correctly uses discreteness of the commutator subgroup and connectedness to conclude triviality.

The commutative multiplication definition and equivalent trivial commutator subgroup are correct. For connected groups, abelian Lie algebra implies locally trivial commutators and hence a discrete commutator subgroup, which connectedness makes trivial; quotient and BCH remarks are correctly scoped.

Differentiating conjugation gives Ad into Lie-algebra automorphisms; in matrix groups it is gXg^{-1}, and Ad(exp X)=exp(ad X). For disconnected G, ker Ad is the centralizer of G°; when G is connected that centralizer is exactly Z(G).

For connected G, the kernel identity follows from the preceding conjugation differentiation argument; discreteness of the kernel is therefore exactly discreteness of Z(G). The distinction between almost effective and effective actions is stated accurately.
The Jacobi identity gives [ad_X,ad_Y]=ad_[X,Y], so ad is a representation; its kernel is exactly the center. The Killing-form trace formula is correctly stated for finite-dimensional Lie algebras.

Finite K-multiplicity is expressed by dim Hom_K(E_tau,V_K)<infinity, with the algebraic and Hilbert formulations distinguished. The caveat that admissibility does not imply finite generation is correct, as is the infinite trivial Hilbert sum counterexample.

The metric definition and connected-group equivalence with Ad-invariance at the identity are correct. The geodesic statement follows from the bi-invariant Levi-Civita connection, and compact averaging supplies existence; the compact semisimple negative Killing form is positive definite.

The page correctly states the compact connected maximal-rank scope, the extended-Dynkin procedure with coefficient 1 or prime coefficient deletion, and the need to restore global central quotients. The F4 examples Spin(9) and (SU(3)×SU(3))/Z3 are consistent with the standard list.

Restriction along a group or algebra homomorphism is defined correctly, with direct-sum notation explicitly conditioned on complete reducibility. The compact-group and semisimple-algebra settings, SO(n−1) example, and global-form caution are all accurate.

The ±1 eigenspace decomposition and bracket inclusions follow directly from θ preserving brackets. The gl_n(R) example gives so(n) and symmetric matrices, and the distinction from root-space decompositions is correct.
The Cartan-involution definition, positive twist, eigenspace decomposition, existence/conjugacy, and gl_n(R) example are consistent with the real reductive convention stated on the page.

The Cartan matrix entries are integers with diagonal 2 and nonpositive off-diagonal entries. The displayed denominator was corrected to (α_i,α_i), matching the repository’s Dynkin-page convention a_ij=<α_i^vee,α_j>; the prior denominator represented the transpose convention.

The characteristic-zero equivalence between semisimplicity and nondegeneracy of the Killing form is stated with the correct quantifiers and standard direct-sum-simple consequence.
The stated characteristic-zero equivalence B(g,[g,g])=0 iff solvability is Cartan’s solvability criterion, with the derived-subalgebra quantifiers and trace formulation correct.

Dual bases for the nondegenerate Killing form give a basis-independent central quadratic element. Scaling B by c scales the inverse tensor by c^{-1}; its action is scalar on irreducibles when Schur’s lemma applies, with normalization-dependent eigenvalue.

The center is correctly defined as a characteristic, closed normal subgroup; for connected G the kernel of Ad is Z(G), matching the preceding adjoint theorem and quotient interpretation.

Because U(g) is generated by g, commuting with every generator characterizes its center. Central elements act as module endomorphisms; the Harish–Chandra polynomial-center statement and PBW invariant-leading-term remark are correctly scoped to complex semisimple g.

entries.evidence: The identity component is an open-and-closed normal embedded subgroup; its cosets are exactly the connected components and the quotient is discrete. The exponential-generation statement is valid because the subgroup generated by any exponential neighborhood is an open subgroup of G^circ, hence all of the connected component.

A connected immersed subgroup is generated by its sufficiently small one-parameter subgroups exp(U∩h), so equal Lie algebras force equal subgroups. The statement correctly says ‘at most one’ for existence and distinguishes uniqueness from the integrability/existence part of Lie correspondence.

The quotient by a closed subgroup has the canonical smooth structure with projection a surjective submersion and smooth transitive left action. The basepoint stabilizer is H, and ker(dπ_e)=h gives T_{eH}(G/H)=g/h as stated.

A covering homomorphism has invertible identity differential and discrete kernel; for connected source, a kernel element commutes with the identity-neighborhood-generated group, hence the kernel is central. Universal covers of connected Lie groups are simply connected Lie groups covering G and are unique over G.

The closed span of the orbit is invariant because π(g) permutes orbit vectors; restriction is cyclic. The zero-vector qualification is correct, and the coefficient is positive-definite. GNS uniqueness for pointed cyclic representations gives exactly the stated reconstruction claim.

The natural inclusion g→gl(V), classical-family table, infinitesimal tensor-preservation equations, omega_1 highest weight, and exterior-power statement for sl_n are correct. The Spin-to-SO vector representation correctly has kernel ±1, clarifying the group/Lie-algebra distinction.

The Leibniz identity for the bracket is correctly stated; commutators of derivations again satisfy it, so Der(g) is a Lie subalgebra. The Jacobi identity proves ad_x is a derivation, and differentiating a one-parameter automorphism family gives a derivation.

Differentiating π(exp(tX)) on the common smooth-vector domain gives a Lie-algebra representation and the stated Ad-equivariance. Smooth vectors are dense and invariant, and their Frechet topology supports the enveloping-algebra module. Stone/Nelson generator facts justify essential skew-adjointness and dπ=iA under the stated convention.

The recursive definition g^(k+1)=[g^(k),g^(k)] is correct. Each term is characteristic, hence an ideal; the solvability/derived-length convention and connected-group infinitesimal analogy are accurate.

The span of brackets is closed under brackets by Jacobi and is an ideal. The abelianization and perfectness consequences follow immediately; a nonabelian simple algebra has nonzero derived ideal and is therefore perfect.
The Jacobi identity expansion [x,[y,z]]=[[x,y],z]+[y,[x,z]] places each term in the span of commutators, proving [g,[g,g]]⊆[g,g]. The contextual characteristic-ideal consequence is accurate.

Pushforward of left-invariant vector fields preserves brackets and evaluates at the identity to dΦ_e, proving bracket preservation. The exponential intertwining follows by uniqueness of one-parameter subgroups and is stated for all X.

The componentwise bracket satisfies the Lie axioms; the two summands commute. A map out of the direct sum is a homomorphism exactly when its two component homomorphism images commute, and Lie(G×H)=Lie(G)⊕Lie(H) is canonical.

The L²(G) closed-summand definition is correct, and for unimodular G the nonzero-L²-matrix-coefficient criterion is the square-integrability characterization. Compact groups give discrete series after normalized Haar measure; Harish-Chandra’s criterion is correctly stated as compact Cartan/rank G=rank K. The noncompact-center obstruction follows from constant coefficient modulus along central cosets.

A subgroup with isolated identity is discrete and closed in a topological group; the closed subgroup theorem makes it embedded, and its Lie algebra is zero. Normal discrete subgroups give Lie-group quotients and covering homomorphisms. The Z^n and ±I examples are valid.

The continuous antilinear dual of H^∞ and inclusions H^∞⊂H⊂H^-∞ are standard for a unitary representation. Enveloping-algebra seminorms describe the smooth Frechet topology, and the inverse action/differentiated minus sign on distribution vectors are correct. The text appropriately distinguishes generalized vectors from Hilbert vectors.

The theorem correctly gives finite sums a*b for C_c^∞(G), and the representation form v=Σπ(f_j)v_j for smooth vectors in continuous Frechet representations. The support-control and finite-sum qualifications are properly stated; the unitary equality with the Gårding span follows as the special case.

A connected complex 1-manifold is a real 2-manifold with holomorphic transitions. The holomorphic-function characterization, automatic biholomorphic inverse for bijective holomorphic maps, canonical orientation via |f'|²>0, and examples are correct.

The pullback metric equality is equivalent to pointwise inner-product preservation; positive definiteness forces injective differential. The distinctions among immersion, embedding, global distance preservation, and holomorphic/Kähler enhancement are correctly stated.

The metric is a smooth positive-definite symmetric 2-tensor, equivalently a tangent-bundle metric. Length, induced distance on components, metric duality, density/volume, Levi–Civita, geodesic and curvature statements, and Euclidean/immersion/pseudo-Riemannian examples are correct.

The constant SO(3) relation between ordered hyperkähler triples is equivalent to the displayed Kähler-form pullback relation (using orthogonality of A). Quaternion multiplication forces orientation preservation; composition and A=I cases are correct, as are the distinctions from generic metric and triholomorphic maps.

For smooth maps between finite-dimensional boundaryless manifolds, critical values are null in target charts; the complement is dense and consists of regular values. The C^k threshold k>max(m−n,0), constant-map example, boundary/infinite-dimensional scope warnings, and distinction between critical points and values are correct.

Scalar curvature is the inverse-metric contraction g^{ij}Ric_{ij}; it is a smooth function and convention-dependent in sign. A single scalar contraction cannot recover the full curvature in dimensions >2, and the conformal-Laplacian/conformal-coupling applications are correctly scoped.

Holomorphic functions on opens form a sheaf by local holomorphicity and unique gluing. Stalks are local C-algebras with maximal ideal of germs vanishing at x and residue field C; chart coordinates identify them with convergent power-series germs. Pullback along holomorphic maps and the ringed-space interpretation are correct.

Smooth functions form a sheaf of real algebras and pointwise smooth functional calculus makes it a sheaf of C-infinity rings. Smooth stalks are local with maximal ideal of germs vanishing at p and residue R; flat nonzero germs show Taylor series do not determine smooth germs. Pullback and local C-infinity ringed-space claims are correct.

With O_alpha carrying the negative KKS form, its moment map is -xi, so the product moment map is μ−xi and zero reduction identifies with μ^{-1}(alpha)/G_alpha. The representative and stabilizer argument proves the set bijection; free/proper regularity gives the symplectic identification, and the sign/singularity caveats are correct.

For compact G, μ^{-1}(0)/G is the singular reduction; orbit-type pieces (and connected components) carry smooth symplectic strata, with natural Poisson structure. The regular/free case recovers Marsden–Weinstein–Meyer, locally free gives orbifolds, and the weighted-circle model and noncompact caveat are correct.

A proper smooth map to [0,∞) has compact sublevels whose union is M, and properness is equivalent to escape-to-infinity of values. Existence on standard second-countable manifolds, R^n and compact examples, and the non-Morse caveat are correct.

Transversality makes the equalizer in M×N an embedded submanifold; the tangent pullback kernel and dimension formula follow from surjectivity of df−dg. Projections satisfy the pullback universal property, and inverse-image/product examples and boundary warning are correct.

A smooth F:M×[0,1]→N with endpoint restrictions is the standard smooth homotopy, with endpoint extension in the boundary direction. The integration homotopy operator gives F_1*−F_0*=dK+Kd, hence equal de Rham maps; isotopy distinction, collar convention, and corners caveat are correct.

The combined map F and each slice F_t are required smooth, with each slice an embedding; therefore isotopy implies smooth homotopy. The embedding/diffeomorphism distinctions, ambient-isotopy description, examples, and isotopy-extension qualification are correct.

Smoothness via local extensions from half-space charts is chart-independent; differential independence, tangent-space dimension at boundary, composition, and absence of automatic boundary preservation are correct. The sqrt(1+x) versus sqrt(x) examples correctly distinguish smooth extension from unbounded derivative.

Joyce smoothness is correctly distinguished from weak chart smoothness by the pullback boundary-defining-function condition (zero or one source boundary factor). Identity/composition/product/inclusion examples and the x² and xy failures are correct under this convention; the convention warning is necessary.

entries.evidence: Reviewed the complete section index: its operator-algebra foundations, positivity, maps, ideals, representations, crossed products, Hilbert modules, von Neumann theory, weights, factors, affiliated operators, and K-theory links are navigational and the listed labels match the linked subjects.

The corner definition pMp abelian is correctly stated; the factor reduction to minimal projections and the B(H) rank-at-most-one example follow from pB(H)p being B(pH). The type-I criterion and distinction from finite projections are correctly scoped.

The inner-product convention, adjoint identity, uniqueness, automatic boundedness, rank-one formula, adjoint formula, compact-operator span, graph-complement characterization, and composition law are mutually consistent for right Hilbert A-modules.

The definition uses a closed densely defined operator and commutation with every unitary in M'; the self-adjoint spectral and polar criteria, multiplication-operator example, and separation of affiliation from measurability/integrability are correctly stated.

For a closed densely defined T with polar decomposition v|T|, the stated equivalence between affiliation, v in M and spectral projections of |T| in M is correct; the resolvent and self-adjoint specializations and closure caveat preserve the required hypotheses.

The locally compact group equivalence among amenability, injectivity of C*(G)->Cr*(G), and equality of full/reduced norms on C_c(G) is correctly stated. Weak-containment, examples, Haar-measure, and discrete-group scope are consistent.

entries.evidence: Read the complete knowl and the four direct prerequisite bodies. The four-positive decomposition and B(H) trace-class model have the stated hypotheses and normalization.

Read the complete knowl and the four direct prerequisite bodies. The preadjoint pairing has the correct direction N_* to M_*; composition reverses correctly. The monotone-supremum characterization is stated only with positivity, and the warning correctly separates ultraweak from automatic norm continuity.

Read the complete knowl and the three direct prerequisite bodies. Positivity plus ultraweak continuity is the stated notion; no unitality, faithfulness, or complete positivity is smuggled in. The preadjoint and increasing-net criterion agree, the ultrafilter state is a valid non-normal example, and composition/scalar-multiple claims follow directly.

Read the complete knowl and the five direct prerequisite bodies. The representation is correctly a normal *-homomorphism into B(H), with faithfulness/unitality separated. Coefficient functionals in M_* give the right normality test; the finite-coordinate projections in ell-infinity provide a correct non-normal ultrafilter character example, and the degenerate/nondegenerate convention is explicit.

The B(H) trace and commutative integration examples satisfy normality, semifiniteness, and faithfulness; a normalized faithful normal state is finite everywhere, while the modular-theory role is accurately scoped.

Read the complete knowl and its three direct prerequisite bodies. The definition correctly adds ultraweak continuity to a *-homomorphism without imposing unitality or injectivity.
